ingredients.name: Leeks
ingredients.notes: large stalks; cut lengthways first to clean sand from between layers, then slice into thin rings

ingredients.name: Maldive fish flakes
ingredients.notes: optional; omit for vegan version; sprinkled at the very end

steps.instruction: Split the leeks in half lengthways first and rinse thoroughly under running water, fanning the layers to wash out any trapped sand or grit. Shake dry, then slice into thin rings, using both the white and the green parts.
Heat the coconut oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them splutter.
Add the sliced onion, garlic, green chillies, curry leaves, and pandan leaf. Saute for about 3-4 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the turmeric and chilli flakes. Stir for 30 seconds.

Add the sliced leeks and a pinch of salt. Toss well to coat in the spice base. Stir-fry over medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the leeks are fully wilted, tender, and slightly caramelised at the edges.
Sprinkle the Maldive fish flakes (if using) over the leeks. Give one final toss. Taste and adjust salt. Serve warm alongside rice and curry.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against loveandotherspices.com, noseychef.com, borntobespicy.com, and TikTok @nipcooks for ingredient list and technique
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 5+ independent sources; strong agreement on the temper-then-stir-fry technique and Maldive fish as the classic optional umami addition
notes: Leek theldala (also called leeks themparaduwa, tempered leeks, or chilli leeks) is one of the most commonly made everyday vegetable side dishes in Sri Lankan homes -- leeks are cheap, widely available, and hold up well to the high-heat stir-fry technique without becoming watery. The defining character is the slightly charred, caramelised edges on the leek pieces, so medium rather than low heat is recommended. Splitting the leek lengthways before washing is non-negotiable -- the layers trap significant amounts of sand and grit that ruins the dish if not washed out. Leeks feature heavily as a signature Sri Lankan ingredient in several other dishes (kottu roti, fried rice, devilled dishes), but this dry, tempered version showcases them as the star on their own.
